title: HOLC Redlining Maps Drawn
description: The Home Owners' Loan Corporation grades Houston neighborhoods A through D. Black and Mexican-American communities in Third Ward, Fifth Ward, and Second Ward are marked 'Hazardous' (D), denying residents access to federally-backed mortgages.

title: Gulf Freeway Construction Begins
description: I-45 South, the first freeway in Texas, begins construction. It will connect downtown Houston to Galveston, establishing the template for highway-driven development.

title: Highways Carve Through East Houston
description: Construction of the East Freeway (I-10 East) begins, cutting through Second Ward and Magnolia Park—neighborhoods already redlined a decade earlier. Hundreds of homes and businesses are demolished.

title: Federal Highway Act Transforms Houston
description: The Federal-Aid Highway Act of 1956 provides 90% federal funding for interstate construction. Houston plans a radial highway network centered on downtown, routing freeways through Black and Hispanic neighborhoods where land is cheapest and political resistance weakest.

title: Southwest Freeway Bisects Third Ward
description: US-59/I-69 construction tears through Third Ward and Midtown, displacing thousands of Black residents. The freeway creates a physical barrier that fragments one of Houston's most established Black communities.

title: Inner Loop Completed
description: I-610 forms a 38-mile loop around central Houston, creating a stark inside/outside divide. Properties inside the loop gain value; communities the loop cuts through—Independence Heights, Eastwood—are disrupted.

title: Civil Rights Act Passes
description: While the Civil Rights Act outlaws racial discrimination, Houston's spatial inequality is already locked in by redlining maps and highway routes. Segregation persists through infrastructure and lending patterns.

title: Petrochemical Boom Along Ship Channel
description: Houston's petrochemical industry expands rapidly along the Ship Channel. Refineries and chemical plants cluster near predominantly Black and Hispanic neighborhoods in East Houston, Manchester, and Galena Park.

title: Tax Day Flood Devastates Meyerland
description: Severe flooding along Brays Bayou inundates the Meyerland neighborhood. Despite repeated floods, development continues in Houston's bayou floodplains with minimal regulation.

title: White Flight and Suburban Expansion
description: Houston's white population increasingly concentrates in suburbs outside Beltway 8—Katy, Sugar Land, Kingwood, Clear Lake. Inner-city neighborhoods see disinvestment as property values and services decline.

title: Oil Bust Hits Houston
description: The collapse of oil prices devastates Houston's economy. Low-income communities of color, already suffering from disinvestment, are hit hardest. Property values in Fifth Ward, Kashmere Gardens, and Sunnyside plummet.

title: EPA Toxics Release Inventory Begins
description: The first TRI data reveals the scale of toxic pollution in East Houston. Communities near the Ship Channel—Manchester, Galena Park, Harrisburg—face some of the highest toxic exposure in the nation.

title: October Flood of 1994
description: Devastating floods along White Oak and Greens Bayous hit northeast Houston hardest—areas that are predominantly Black and Hispanic. FEMA buyout programs begin acquiring properties in flood-prone areas.

title: Tropical Storm Allison
description: Allison drops 40 inches of rain on Houston in June 2001, causing $9 billion in damage. The Medical Center floods catastrophically. Low-income areas along bayous suffer worst, with the least resources to recover.

title: Gentrification Accelerates in Inner Loop
description: Heights, Montrose, EaDo, and Midtown see rapid development. Property values soar, pricing out long-time residents. Areas once redlined as 'hazardous' become desirable—but for new, wealthier, whiter populations.

title: Houston Becomes Majority-Minority
description: Houston is now one of the most ethnically diverse large cities in America. But diversity and integration are different things—racial and economic segregation patterns from the 1940s remain starkly visible.

title: Tax Day Flood & Memorial Day Flood
description: Two devastating floods hit Houston in April and May 2016. Meyerland floods for the third time in 18 months. Low-income communities in Greens Bayou watershed, already living with industrial pollution, face repeated flood damage.

title: Hurricane Harvey
description: Harvey drops over 60 inches of rain on Houston—the most extreme rainfall event in US history. Over 300,000 structures flood. Recovery reveals deep inequality: wealthier neighborhoods rebuild quickly while low-income communities of color wait years for assistance. Superfund sites overflow, spreading toxins into neighboring communities.

title: Inequality Persists
description: In 2020, the median household income in River Oaks exceeds $250,000 while in Fifth Ward it's under $28,000—a 9:1 ratio. Life expectancy varies by up to 25 years between Houston ZIP codes. The map of inequality today still echoes the HOLC maps of 1940.
